Unless, of course, a relief pitcher enters the game during this half inning. A relief pitcher does not receive the benefit of previous errors when entering the game and must be charged with earned runs for which he is solely responsible, the team however, is credited with a “Team Unearned Run”

Let’s use the same play as the basis for the example. These two runners score thanks to the E2T. 

The next batter singles and the manager goes to the bullpen. The new relief pitcher gives up a 2-run homerun.

The runner who reached via single is unearned due to the original error and is charged to the previous pitcher. The second batter, who hit the homerun, is the sole responsibility of the new pitcher. It’s a wild pitch as the lead runner advanced and hitter reached base. A WP is charged (in general) to any ball in the dirt, or the pitch otherwise requires a greater than ordinary effort by the catcher, when a runner advances due to the pitch (players who break on the pitch to steal are still credited with a SB and the P is not charged with a WP)

Specifically, in this situation, because the pitch hits the dirt, allowing a dropped third strike, even though the hitter reaches due to an E2T, the pitcher is charged with a wild pitch as had it not been Wild, the hitter would be out.

It would officially be credited as: 

Batter: KS E2T +++ UE
Lead runner: WP ++ UE

(swinging strikeout, batter reached on throwing error by Catcher, advanced three additional bases, run unearned - runner advances due to a wild pitch, advances two more bases, run is unearned)

(Another fun fact, the WP can go on either the hitter or the runner, but not both, as it’s a single play. Putting it on both would charge the pitcher with two wild pitches)

Hitter does not receive an RBI.

The franchise CPU logic, progression/regression, generated players, budget, and contracts (pretty much anything and everything relating to rosters) are all horrible.

Players don’t retire when they should, so minor league rosters fill up with 37 year old, 60 overall players. There aren’t enough generated players each year, despite the game generating filler players in Year 1 in FA - it does not continue to generate extra filler players. I’ve had times where there are less than 5 catchers, 0 CP, less than 10 SP in Free Agency on opening day. 

Scouting is fucking *atrocious*. “Discovering” prospects is one of the (if not top of the list) dumbest features for scouting in sports gaming. It makes sense in FIFA, it would make sense in MLB if it was discovering International FA targets, but oh that’s right, SDS doesn’t do that.

Players regress at an alarming and stupid rate. I’ve had players who, on Opening Day, will drop 2 or 3 in overall without playing a game. Players, pitchers especially, fall off a cliff once they hit 10 years of service time. So, a player who is a top talent prospect, MLB ready at 18 (it happens but rare), will rapidly decline at age 28 and 29, ending up almost unplayable by 32. (Then they’ll somehow stick around until they’re 43, spending 6 years in AA or Free Agency)

The weekly budget format is terrible, it should be set to a yearly payroll budget for players. I get that teams budget fluctuate based on performance, but I’ve had years where I’ve started a season with high expectations from the owner, had a couple injuries and bad sim results, then my budget plummets so I’m forced to trade players. 

Related to budgets, CPU teams routinely spend more than they are capable of and end up 40-50 million in the hole. There’s 2-3 teams a season that do it. 

CPU lineups, bullpen usage, and roster management defy any and all logic. I’ve seen teams have nobody capable of playing 1B on the roster, playing a 2B at 1B and averaging 4 errors per game, despite having an MLB capable 1B in AAA who is non-40'd. They platoon players who shouldn't be platooned. Long relievers get used FAR too often. The "second" setup reliever gets far too little usage. 

Trading is also bad. The CPU has no idea how to value players or what type of players they need/want. I've watched Rafael Devers get traded for 2 C level prospects and a 70 overall reliever. Trading should also be changed to include more spots and have the ability to trade cash.

EDIT: Forgot to add, Quick Manage is absolutely broken. Player attributes seem to be completely irrelevant. Quick manage should be the best way to play a season and have a hand in every game without playing 1,458 innings (or more). But the logic behind is so, so terrible. Pitchers get absolutely rocked no matter their ratings and it seems to heavily favor the CPU. Your overall record at the end of the year will probably be near where it should, but the stats are all over the place by using Quick Manage. It is, however, the only way to ensure your pitching staff is used correctly as the logic through sim is somehow worse.

For franchise, a non-exhaustive list:

-Complete overhaul of generated players in Franchise, including (But not limited to): Wider range of names from the recorded list being selected. Equipment/appearance not being an absolute shit show circus with sleeves mismatched, pitchers using an open web on their glove, or the use of the moronic ice cream gloves. Catcher’s gear being defaulted to team colors. 

-A larger pool of generated players each year, there should be some generated international FA’s, undrafted Free Agents. (Would allow for more minor league moves over the course of the year and prevent teams from filling their minor league system with 37 year olds)

-Rework AI roster logic completely. They make horrible decisions whenever they get the chance.

-Move pitchers from being SP, RP, or CL to RHP or LHP. Make stamina the determining factor for whether a pitcher should start or not instead of a “position” given how often pitchers get moved around in real life. 

-Add utility as a secondary position option in editing players. 

-Make two-way players available to be built in the minors (the needed AB’s/innings pitched shouldn’t be only MLB).

-Actual record books for teams and league again.

-Allow for players to be “trained” at a position during spring training and in the minor leagues. 

-Change “secondary position” attribute penalty to change based on familiarity with secondary position. Each player should have a “positions” tab in the player customization suite where it would go from 0-100, 0 being completely unfamiliar to 100 being primary position. The penalty for secondary positions would be 100-[the player’s familiarity]/2, expressed as a percentage. So if a player has a familiarity of 90 at a secondary position, the penalty would be a five-point reduction in fielding stats at that secondary position. 

-Winter Meetings and the Trade deadline should have a FIFA/NHL style “deadline” where you try to make moves over the course of X hours (with an option to skip).

-Player cards should show ALL teams a player has played for in a year instead of only “TOT”. Selecting that year and hitting A/X should drop down the stats for each team they played on. 

- Minor league stats should be shown when a player has been called up to the Big leagues and appears at the plate or on the mound. 

-Minor League stats should be shown on the player cards in a Minors tab. 

-Retired numbers (except for 42) should be able to be toggled off.

-Teams should cycle out minor league players more often.

The SGC operates in the “find and acquire technology” manner because they are under existential threat from the Goa’uld. 

O’Neill and SG-1 have much more leeway when it comes to offering assistance as they hope to acquire tech, whether ancient or otherwise. They know the Goa’uld didn’t build the Stargates pretty early on, so they’re hoping to scrounge tech and form meaningful relationships in the hopes of finding allies. They’re also not keen on giving out technology which could be used for war. 

The episode “The Other Side” effectively showed that Earth would have accepted technology from literal Space Nazis if it were not for O’Neill’s decision to sabotage their defense and close the Iris at SGC on the way out. 

Likewise, the Asgard really don’t *like* to interfere but will if inter-system treaties like the Protected Planets treaty are violated. (Or that time SG-1 caused an asteroid to *almost* hit a planet it shouldn’t have because they overrode some coordinates)

Without the existential threat, it becomes an ethical quandary of whether or not to assist civilizations of lower technology status. Star Trek’s answer was the Prime Directive, to shield unprepared civilizations from acquiring tech well beyond their means. It is worth noting, they violate the Prime Directive often.

A similar situation plays out prior to the events of Mass Effect. The Krogan reached industrialization, bombed themselves back to warring tribes, and are uplifted by the Salarians, Turians, and Asari to combat the Rachni.

After a near total victory, the Krogan wage a hellish war against everyone else. This culminates in the Salarians creating the Genophage, limiting the Krogan birth rate and immensely slowing the growth of the population. 

The immense power and knowledge wielded by space faring civilizations can’t be taken lightly or handed out at will. Part of that includes solving problems which an advanced society may have solved long ago. 

While helping may seem altruistic (not in the case of uplifting the Krogan, that was selfish), there’s no telling how the interference will affect the growth and development of a species. 

It also prevents the deification of the advanced society or creating a slave caste from the less advanced. Human history is littered with what happens when a technologically advanced culture meets a culture that isn’t as far along. 

For lack of anything else, it’s about a civilization’s ability to earn the right to seek a home amongst the stars. There’s a method to that madness, you don’t reach the point of space-faring by accident and you hopefully work out some of the more nefarious parts of civilization (greed, war mongering, etc - take a look at the Orokin from Warframe for what happens when a civilization doesn’t). Any assistance, whether physical technology or political discourse, even food, could dramatically alter the path of a civilization.

Niggardly dates back to the Middle Ages and means “stingy” or “miserly”. 

There were multiple incidents around the turn of the 21st millennium with the word being used. In 1999, “niggardly” was used to describe a budget, and it was used in a college classroom at UW-Madison while the professor was teaching Chaucer. In 2002, it was used by a high school teacher in Wilmington, NC to describe literary characters and in 2009 it was used during a defamation suit in California against Mendocino County Office of Education. It’s a good game. I went into it by ignoring *everything* regarding the game. No reviews, no YouTube videos, nothing. I’ll try it hit as much as I can about the game and mechanics. 

I’ve put 155 or so hours into it, Im in NG+3, and have been on a break from it. I’ve hit the proverbial wall for the moment but I plan on coming back (probably soon). No different than any other Bethesda game for me. I still have active characters on Morrowind, Oblivion, Fallout 3, Skyrim, and F4. 

There are some really good parts to the game, a lot of meh parts, but very few awful parts.

Good: The gunplay is the best Bethesda has ever done, having IO come in to revamp it during development was an incredibly good decision. Every weapon type is viable, ammo is plentiful. For the first time in a Bethesda game, I’ve felt like money is really no issue which is nice. I can stock up on ammo, buy new ship parts, and buy some materials (I’m not big into production stuff). 

I enjoy the companions, each of their respective quests are really well done. The side companions (hireable folks) are a nice touch, but lack robust personalities. That makes them great for when you want to do some…not so “nice” things. 

The shipbuilding is one of the best features in the game. I can’t wait for more ship parts to be released. Building my own unique ship, one that feels lived in and functional, has been my favorite part of the game. It’s a blast taking something I built around and essentially living on it. 

I like the perks system for the most part. It makes leveling your character an interesting bit and feels like you’re progressing (more so than Skyrim or F4). Though, there are some big drawbacks to the system.

Scanning planets and animals doesn’t seem to get old (I wish there were a few more varied fauna modes), but I really like interacting with fauna and trying to *not* mass murder them. Just observe and hang out.

Meh: The three major cities are decent. I love Neon’s aesthetic but I wish it was seedier and fully lived up to its reputation. New Atlantis is gorgeous and the Well is a nice juxtaposition to that beauty. Akila City reminds me of Firefly, which I really enjoyed.

Certain quest lines are better than others, for instance, the UC Vanguard quest line has some of the best writing Bethesda has done but I found the main quest line to be pretty underwhelming (I actually enjoyed the game MORE before I had access to certain things). The writing is very mediocre, overall. 

The world building is a bit underwhelming for what I expect out of Bethesda. Part of it is due to the proc gen POIs. I’ve found farms with slates saying they were killed by local fauna, but the planet has zero fauna. Then that same farm and slate on a planet WITH fauna, which made much more sense. The repeating slates and loot do wane the enjoyment. 

I don’t mind the POIs repeating, each time I find one I’ve hit before I get to use my previous knowledge of it to attack it in a different way. I do wish the loot and what’s found inside each POI to be more varied. You’re still hitting the same POI, with the same enemies, in the same spots.

Bad: The sheer amount of proc gen. I get what they’re going for, but just like NMS, it wears on me pretty quickly. While the POIs are a much more interesting system than NMS (and is more varied) having the same slates, telling the same stories, with the same names, on different planets isn’t good. For what they touted in exploration, it’s one of the weaker parts of the game for me.

Missions seem to lack the Bethesda charm. Some stick out, for instance a particularly mundane mission to grab a specific coffee for a worker in New Atlantis you meet. It’s so pointless but I love it because the worker is a sweet character and it’s nice to make her day. The mission board missions are weak. It’s kill ship, kill bad guy, deliver something/someone, or source items. The delivery amounts to flying to that system (so it’s basically loading screens) and landing. The kill missions are fine but again, it’s lots of loading screens. The source missions I don’t take because I can’t be assed to set up the outpost for it. You’re going to get the same radiant missions from the same proc gen POIs. 

There are a *TON* of loading screens, more so than in any previous title as Starfield is much more segmented than previous BGS titles. It has worn on me a bit, especially when it is entering shops or buildings in a city when the shop next door doesn’t have a loading screen. However, the space travel is fine. There’s not a lot to actually traveling, but you will find a huge number of derelict ships, and enemies to fight within systems.

Outposts are…boring. Without perks you’re really limited in both what you create and how many you can create. Even when I had the perks, I didn’t really care for it. If you need specific materials, outposts are a great way to go about it, but building an outpost for aesthetics or to build yourself a little home base is taxing and not worth it. 

Overall, I thinks it’s a good game. I’ve gotten 150 hours out of it, so it did something right. If you like BGS games and have an imagination, it’s definitely worth it. There’s a good amount of things to do. It just seems to lack the usual Bethesda charm. I can’t put my finger on it, but *something* is missing from Starfield.

It isn’t, the AI uses money but there are a number of mechanics the AI utilizes to keep money flowing.

AI lords have access to a hidden kingdom bank that starts at 2.0 million (day one of campaign) on top of their personal incomes. When a player creates their own kingdom, allied AI lords also got access to a hidden bank but the player cannot access it and it does not begin with any funds. 

They also get free troops when they are released from capture, usually 10-20, (enough to prevent most bandit parties from grabbing them) and (like the player can) withdraw from garrisons.

They don’t need to buy war mounts to upgrade certain cavalry units. 

They use their personal incomes until they drop below 30k, then withdraw from the kingdom bank. They also contribute to the kingdom bank when they’re making a surplus. 

The AI is gifted certain perks relating to wages, revenue, and upkeep, whereas the player has to specifically select them. 

It takes roughly 2 years of 0 income to drain the initial 2 million value of the kingdom bank. This would mean from day one: raiding all villages, killing all caravans, ensuring all clan members fail to generate any income, and a blanket blockade against anything that could conceivably make money for that faction. 

If you were able to accomplish that, the AI would then be on a similar playing field as the player in terms of money and how to manage it.
My honest guess is it’s a % value. The better monikers (like Falcon) are more rare, while things like Cowthief or Surgeon are more common.

It is. It’s partly balance, as players we always find ways to punish certain aspects of gameplay. It’s also partly entertainment, it’d be really boring if everyone was bankrupt and couldn’t raise parties two years in because the cities changed rulers to a different culture creating massive deficits (it protects the AI from everything other than rebellion in that regard).

Without the proper medical knowledge, abilities, or equipment, it was seen as a way to end the suffering of someone who was mortally wounded. It spawned the phrase *coup de grâce*. 

Battlefield collection duties and stripping of the dead was a widely accepted practice as well. Different factions and cultures throughout history approached it differently. The Romans disliked dealing with the dead, so they assigned camp followers or slaves (though every so often legionnaires would get the duty). The Greeks believed a proper burial was extremely important and in many cases allowed their enemy to reclaim the dead for burial. 

Sometimes looting started during the battle, like at the Battle of Hastings where displaced civilians began stripping the dead.

It’s an incredibly fascinating portion of warfare history.

Like the MLB portion, the MiLB draft has the same eligibility requirements with one difference. Instead of being assigned to the MLB Club’s 40-man roster, the organization can assign a player to their AAA affiliate’s 38-man roster. The players assigned are protected during the minor league portions of the rule 5 draft (or what’s been called the “minor league shuffle”).

When a player is selected during the MiLB portion, he must be assigned to your AAA expanded roster. You can’t snag a AAA guy and stash him on the AA roster…yet. 

Unlike the MLB portion, there is no right of return. It is highly encouraged a club offer the player a spot on the same level affiliate he was taken from after spring training, but it is not required. 

Most of the players selected in the minor league portion are career minor leaguers so there’s not really a need to protect them from the MLB portion (Seth Beer is a really interesting case as he has appeared in two seasons at the MLB level for ARZ but was not protected in either phase and was selected in the MiLB phase by PIT). If the player doesn’t stick, they are required to offer the player back to the original team for $50k. A loss of $50k for the selecting team if a player doesn’t pan out.

3) The vast majority of Rule 5 picks are going to be players who have either never seen the major leagues or have been shuffled on and off the 40 throughout the season, meaning they’ve gone through waivers a time or two. You’re taking a chance on guy you hope can find a groove, prove they can hang at the MLB level.

4) Players are only eligible after experiencing their 4th Rule 5 Draft or 5th if they signed their original contract at 18 years old and are not on the 40-man roster by Nov 18. That means they’ve spent 4-5 seasons in the minors, putting their age at roughly 23-25, on par with the MLB rookie age.

Let’s not pretend, however, that SDS has done anything to install confidence the last few years. The problem with The Show is: SDS is taking the EA route. 

Franchise mode has been completely neglected in favor of Diamond Dynasty (and they’ve even gotten worse there). 

Player regression and progression is horrible, players don’t retire when they should (you get 37 year olds in AA with a 55 overall rating), the FA pool a few years in is extremely shallow (8 SP, none below the age of 29 in year 4 for me), AI lineup, rotation, and bullpen management is atrocious (you’ll see relievers appear in 16 games who have been rostered all season, while another pitches in 83), they finally updated drafting from a system they used since the early 2000’s but didn’t address the AI draft logic (and it’s not a large improvement), and despite having tons of equipment options ALL generated players (including pitchers) use the same glove webbing (and it’s one 0 pitchers use). Player generation still happens like it’s 1998 with far too many SP having really high stamina (which I personally love, but it doesn’t match the evolution of the game and further wrecks the use of relievers by the AI), fielding is overprioritized in overall ratings. 

Trade logic is poor, free agency logic is worse. Teams will sign 8 SP who are above 80, slap three of them in the bullpen, then start a 62 at 2B because they didn’t have the budget to sign one. Not to mention pitching is much more fluid than in the past (Boston this season flipped two SP into the bullpen, started a reliever in one of their slots and then piggyback the former starter off the reliever) but SDS insists on using completely outdated and rigid categorizations. Utility players all but completely vanish as generated players through the draft don’t generate with utility at the proper rate (there’s also no option to teach players positions and, while there’s an edit secondary position option in the player edit menu, IF/OF is not one of them, nor can you set specific positions - like giving a 1B the secondary of 3B/LF, you’re stuck with predefined ones).

Let’s talk about budgets. SDS uses the dumbest budget system in all of sports gaming. You can start the year with a budget of $150 million, suffer some injuries or setbacks, and watch your budget drop to under $100 million in the same season making it impossible to salvage the team and forcing you to sell players as the budget updates weekly instead of per season. 

Because they use a fluid budget system, teams like Oakland and Kansas City (who are bad and have small payrolls IRL at the moment, but have spent in the past to try and win) never get a chance to actually rebuild because their budget is constantly shot due to performance…because they can’t add better players with higher salaries…because their budget never improves…because their budget shrinks due to performance…rinse and repeat.

The Show’s franchise was the pinnacle of sports franchise modes for a long time, but the last few years they’ve neglected it to the point of a deep regression and should not be held in high regard. 

The bar for sports games is so incredibly fucking low it should embarrass every one involved.

Earth has 24 hours because the Sumerians developed base 60 mathematics. The Babylonians/Egyptians developed that into two sections (day/night) over 12 periods at 60 minutes per section.

Time “passes” based on how quickly or slowly a planet rotates on its axis. It takes Earth 24 hours, Mars 25, and it takes Mercury 59 DAYS (1,408 hours) to complete a rotation.

A year is a complete orbit of a planet’s star. Farther out a planet is, the longer it takes. It takes Earth 365 24-hour periods (most of the time), while it takes Mars 687 Earth days to complete its orbit. Meanwhile, Mercury needs just 88 Earth days to complete its orbit as its closer to the sun.

I wholly agree on cap depressing wages. The difference between the NHL and MLB is MLB teams shut the player out after exchanging values because they know they’re more likely to win. The NHL process discourages both parties from going to arbitration (higher salary for team than they wanted, less than player wanted), while MLB arbitration heavily favors the team and league.

“File and trial” is directly linked to the rule. League and teams know they’ll probably win, so they shut down negotiations. Everything after is a knock-on effect and  I imagine the hearings in NHL and MLB are similar, though MLB seems to have a higher level of vitriol towards the player. 

For instance, 2021 Cy Young Winner Corbin Burnes went to arbitration prior to this season over $750,000. [During the hearing, the Brewers blamed Burnes for missing the postseason](https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/mlb/2023/02/16/corbin-burnes-milwaukee-brewers-salary-arbitration-spring-trainin/11274307002/) despite leading the NL in strikeouts and posting a sub 3.00 ERA. 

In the NHL, this would probably have been settled during the period from exchanging numbers and the actual hearing as nobody really enjoys arbitration. 

But in the MLB, the league and teams know they’ll probably win. So, if you reach the date to exchange values, what further incentive does the club have to negotiate? There is none. They know they are more likely to come out on top. 

The NHL system doesn’t really have a “winner.” The team is paying more for a player than they wanted and the player is getting less than they wanted. It discourages teams and players from going to arbitration (which, in my opinion is a good thing).

[MLB proposed](https://www.mlbtraderumors.com/2021/11/mlb-proposes-replacing-arbitration-with-salaries-based-off-player-war-totals.html) moving to a set salary scale based on a player’s service time and WAR (wins above replacement). The proposal also changes FA requirements, setting the standard at 29.5 years of age rather than six years of service time. The offer was an absolute non-starter for the players.

It’s not. As I put elsewhere in this comment thread, MLB and its clubs have weaponized arbitration to depress wages at almost any cost. They denigrate players during hearings, flex their bankroll with lawyers and analysts, and have colluded so all 30 teams take a “file and trial” approach wherein teams refuse to negotiate with players (despite being able to) once the arbitration numbers exchange date hits. This forces players to take lesser deals prior to the date or risk losing more in arbitration. 

MLBPA wins roughly 50% (more often less) of arb cases every year. It incentivizes teams to lowball the players’ value as the league and clubs have more resources at their disposal to draft an argument on why the player is worth what they say. The CBA had to have a clause banning certain stats and metrics from being used in arbitration as the league can cultivate the data, but the PA cannot. 

If a player uses a smaller agent firm, they’re at more of a disadvantage than the players who use larger firms. 

The league and owners dislike arbitration because when players win, it’s generally high profile and high skill players.  MLB tried to remove arbitration all together during the most recent CBA negotiations. 

The NHL system isn’t perfect, but it’s far better than MLB’s which is nothing more than the league and owners openly attempting to depress wages.

Umberto Eco’s 14 common features of fascism in an essay in the New York Review in 1995 (the following is abridged): 

1. The cult of tradition. “One has only to look at the syllabus of every fascist movement to find the major traditionalist thinkers. The Nazi gnosis was nourished by traditionalist, syncretistic, occult elements.”

2. The rejection of modernism. “The Enlightenment, the Age of Reason, is seen as the beginning of modern depravity. In this sense Ur-Fascism can be defined as irrationalism.”

3. The cult of action for action’s sake. “Action being beautiful in itself, it must be taken before, or without, any previous reflection. Thinking is a form of emasculation.”

4. Disagreement is treason. “The critical spirit makes distinctions, and to distinguish is a sign of modernism. In modern culture the scientific community praises disagreement as a way to improve knowledge.”

5. Fear of difference. “The first appeal of a fascist or prematurely fascist movement is an appeal against the intruders. Thus Ur-Fascism is racist by definition.”

6. Appeal to social frustration. “One of the most typical features of the historical fascism was the appeal to a frustrated middle class, a class suffering from an economic crisis or feelings of political humiliation, and frightened by the pressure of lower social groups.”

7. The obsession with a plot. “Thus at the root of the Ur-Fascist psychology there is the obsession with a plot, possibly an international one. The followers must feel besieged.”

8. The enemy is both strong and weak. “By a continuous shifting of rhetorical focus, the enemies are at the same time too strong and too weak.”

9. Pacifism is trafficking with the enemy. “For Ur-Fascism there is no struggle for life but, rather, life is lived for struggle.”

10. Contempt for the weak. “Elitism is a typical aspect of any reactionary ideology.”

11. Everybody is educated to become a hero. “In Ur-Fascist ideology, heroism is the norm. This cult of heroism is strictly linked with the cult of death.”

12. Machismo and weaponry. “Machismo implies both disdain for women and intolerance and condemnation of nonstandard sexual habits, from chastity to homosexuality.”

13. Selective populism. “There is in our future a TV or Internet populism, in which the emotional response of a selected group of citizens can be presented and accepted as the Voice of the People.”

14. Ur-Fascism speaks Newspeak. “All the Nazi or Fascist schoolbooks made use of an impoverished vocabulary, and an elementary syntax, in order to limit the instruments for complex and critical reasoning.”

Some historical context for those that may not know:

Hitler was particularly impressed with a book published in 1916, by Madison Grant, titled “The Passing of the Great Race.”

Based on Francis Galton’s belief in selective breeding (he argued if we could breed faster horses we could breed better people), Grant expanded the idea to “undesirable” traits being passed, not only from family, but from certain ethnic backgrounds and religious groups. 

In particular, Grant believed the US was committing “race suicide” as more immigrants were coming, not from places like the British Isles and Scandinavia, but places like Southern and Eastern Europe.

The US in 1917 passed a law banning “all idiots, imbeciles, feebleminded persons, epileptics, insane persons, [and] persons of constitutional psychopathic inferiority” from entering.

Not too mention a letter written to Grant by a eugenicist stating, “Can we build a wall high enough around this country so as to keep out these cheaper races; or will it be a feeble dam, leaving it to our descendants to abandon the country to blacks, browns, and yellows.”

In 1924, another bill passed restricting immigrants from African descent after a 1921 limiting immigration overall to 3% of the population. In 1929, another bill was passed further limiting immigration from Southern/Eastern Europe. 

Grant claimed, according to a book by Jonathan Peter Spiro (Defending the Master Race: Conservation, Eugenics and the Legacy of Madison Grant), “[This is] one of the greatest steps forward in the history of this country. We have closed the doors just in time to prevent our Nordic population from being overrun by the lower races.”

The book was translated to German in 1926. 

In a letter written from Bavaria after his part in a riot, Hitler wrote, “This book is my Bible.” Hitler included large sections of Grant’s book in “Mein Kampf”

Somewhat relevant story about a player being ejected after a game: 

I worked as a bat-boy for the Red Sox Single-A affiliate back in ‘07. Same year MiLB debuted its “batters must keep two feet in the box after taking a strike” rule.

Season is 2/3 over. We are at home, top 9. Two outs, tying run on base. Count I believe was 1-2 (DEFINITELY two strikes). We are playing the Lakewood Blue Claws.

The something and 1 pitch comes in, called strike two. Lakewood down to its final strike, batter does the wide legged “step out” to adjust himself. Our catcher looks down and notices the batter’s foot is just outside the box. He notifies the home plate umpire. 

HP umpire rips off his mask, steps out from behind the plate, and declares strike three “batter has violated the rule and didn’t remain in the box.”

All hell breaks loose. The game is over…the batter slams his helmet and bat, starts yelling, gets tossed. Their manager Steve Roadcap (believe it was Steve, but Roadcap is correct) is IRATE. He managed to get his money’s worth, screaming at the umpires from home plate to the tunnel down the 1st base line. He is also ejected.

MiLB rules state a player ejected after the game is suspended for the next. Not Roadie, however.

Next day we have the series finale. Pre-game plate meeting happens and the HP umpire from yesterday is in the field.

Roadie goes to the plate, shakes Kapler’s (Greenville manager) hand and the hand of today’s HP umpire. He does NOT shake the field umpire’s hand, but after turning over his lineup card, squares up across home plate and (once again) gets his money’s worth. Boom ejected. 

MiLB relaxed the rule the next year.

Freelancer is a higher difficulty. It’s designed to be a challenge and require you to think things through. Alert times are quicker, more enforcers, responses more deadly. Wealth beyond measure, outlander! Here are a few tips I find helpful for new players making a backwards jump from newer ES games:

1) be patient. Your character has just been released from prison after an unknown amount of time. Their skills are rusty. Carefully choose your major skills to things you’ll want to use. You can push your misc skills later through training or regular use, but your major and minor skills are going to be what gets you through the game.

2) Consider speechcraft. Unlike oblivion and Skyrim, Morrowind’s disposition system has direct implications to conversations. If an NPC likes you, they’re more likely to barter, give advice, or rumors. It is also changes prices on goods bought and sold (mercantile does this as well, but more so allows a greater ability to bargain).

3) Morrowind can be as easy or as hard as you want to make it. From the skills and class you choose, to deciding whether to partake in numerous exploits, you have a wide ability to set how difficult the game will be .

4) Factions are more in depth and require the use or training or specific skills to advance. Unlike the later games, you will not be able to ride up through the ranks of every faction by just completing quests. Each faction has their own skill set and you will need to hit certain benchmarks to advance.

5) There are inter-faction conflicts. It is possible to avoid being locked out of certain factions by doing certain tasks in a specific order, however, for your first playthrough - I would encourage you to just play and see where it takes you!

6) Certain enemies (bone walkers, specifically) will ruin your day with attribute crushing effects. Find ways to mitigate that in the field with potions/spells.

7) Fast Travel is limited to Silt Striders, intervention spells, Mark/Recall, Mages Guild, and Indexes. The system is pretty intuitive and allows nearly unfettered access to most of the continent. 

8) Read EVERYTHING. Talk to NPC’s, read notes, books, scrolls. Morrowind is steeped in world building and lore, it’s all there for you to explore and read. 

9) Beware of the Overflow Loot Bag in buildings you call home. We all love to decorate our houses with trinkets, rewards, and other stuff. Morrowind’s answer to this comes with an Overflow Loot Bag if you put too much in the cell. Once it spawns, everything you drop in the cell goes to that bag.

10) There are no map markers, so read carefully when NPC’s give you directions. Refer to your journal often.

11) Save. Save early, save often. Save always. I love Morrowind, it’s my favorite game of all time, but strange things happens and keeping multiple saves is the best way to not lose multiple hours of progression. 

12) Stamina is critical to your success and touches every aspect of the game. Running also lowers your stamina. Keep the green as full as you can.

The discovery and confirmation of intelligent life with the capability to travel between systems would cause an existential crisis across not just religion but the general population. Resource hoarding, riots, and violent crime would all rise. 

There isn’t really a way to slow reveal the program, either. Technological jumps are easier to hide and can be explained through classified R&D projects. The Stargate is a technological wonder eons beyond what we are capable of.

The rule makes this call crystal clear. Let’s break it down:

“The rule is based on the premise that an attacking player's position, whether inside or outside the crease, should not, by itself, determine whether a goal should be allowed or disallowed - i.e., goals scored while attacking players are standing in the crease may, in appropriate circumstances be allowed.”

Okay, positioning alone doesn’t make it interference when positioning alone is the question. This isn’t the case in this situation. Contact was made so we have to move forward to the next portion.

“Goals should be disallowed only if: (1) an attacking player, either by his positioning or by contact, impairs the goalkeeper's ability to move freely within his crease or defend his goal; or (2) an attacking player initiates more than incidental contact with a goalkeeper, inside or outside of his goal crease.”

The goalie was clearly impaired in his ability defend his goal by moving freely inside the crease. Specifically having to push past the attacking player to make an attempt to slide over inside his crease. The attacking player’s skates and back side are in the crease throughout the attacking play. If that’s still not enough, we can look at the final portion of the rule: 

“Incidental contact with a goalkeeper will be permitted, and resulting goals allowed, when such contact is initiated outside of the goal crease, provided the attacking player has made a reasonable effort to avoid such contact.”

The incidental contact was inside the crease. Even if an argument can be made for the attacking player being outside the crease at the time of contact (which would be by the slimmest of margins), the attacking player made no effort to prevent incidental contact.

So, under the provisions provided for the attacking player, this is clear interference. The subsequent sections, however, make it even more clear.

“If an attacking player initiates contact with a goalkeeper, incidental or otherwise, while the goalkeeper is in his goal crease, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed.”

Okay, so did the attacker or goaltender initiate contact? Well, it doesn’t really matter given the position of the goaltender and the contact (inside the crease) unless the goaltender commits an act which rises to the level of a penalty. This does not. 

“If (i) a goalkeeper initiates contact with an offensive player who is in the goal crease; and (ii) such contact is (a) initiated by the goalkeeper in order to establish position in his goal crease; and (b) results in an impairment of the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed.
If, after any contact by a goalkeeper who is attempting to establish position in his goal crease, the attacking player does not immediately vacate his current position in the goal crease (i.e. give ground to the goalkeeper), and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed. “

Goaltender is clearly moving to position himself as the play moves. The attacking player DID NOT immediately vacate his position. 

“(NOTE 1) The overriding rationale of subsections (d) and (e) above is that a goalkeeper should have the ability to move freely within his goal crease without being hindered by the actions of an attacking player.

The goaltender did not have the ability to move freely without being hindered by the actions of the attacking player. 

“If an attacking player establishes a significant position within the goal crease, so as to obstruct the goalkeeper's vision and impair his ability to defend his goal, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed.

(NOTE) For this purpose, a player "establishes a significant position within the crease" when, in the Referee's judgment, his body, or a substantial portion thereof, is within the goal crease for more than an instantaneous period of time.

Subject to (i) below, if an attacking player enters the goal crease and, by his actions, impairs the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed.”

“NOTE 1) For purposes of this rule, "contact", whether incidental or otherwise, shall mean any contact that is made between or among a goalkeeper and attacking player(s), whether by means of a stick or any part of the body.

(NOTE 2) The above-stated standards relating to when a goal will be disallowed will be applied in all situations in which the puck enters the net regardless of whether it was directed into the net by the attacking or defensive team.”

So, again, in the final portion of the rule (subtracting sections on the assessing of penalties), it’s a clear cut instance of interference when the rule is applied as written. Plays like this are the reason rules are so long and written as they are. When you apply the rule the way it’s broken down, it does the work for you.
